---
title: "CLT Convergence for Six-Sided Die"
format: html
editor: visual
---

## Background

The distributions being averaged here are the results of rolling a six-sided die. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are the only possible outcomes of each roll, and they are equally likely. The results being strictly bounded will likely result in faster convergence, as there are no strong outliers to affect the means, and the distribution is already symmetric.

## Data

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# Monte Carlo Simulation: Fair Six-Sided Die Parent (Discrete Uniform)
# ==============================================================================

library(ggplot2)

# 1. Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6418)

# 2. Simulation parameters
B <- 10000                            # Number of Monte Carlo repetitions
n_values <- c(2, 5, 10, 30, 100)      # Sample sizes to test

# 3. Initialize storage
results <- data.frame()
sim_data <- list()                    # List to store raw sample means vectors

# 4. Run Monte Carlo loop for Fair Six-Sided Die
for (n in n_values) {
  
  # Draw B sample means from rolling n fair six-sided dice
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE)))
  
  # Save raw sample means for visual validation graphs
  sim_data[[as.character(n)]] <- sample_means
  
  # A. Calculate Q-Q Plot R-squared
  theo_quantiles <- qnorm(ppoints(B))
  sample_quantiles <- sort(sample_means)
  r2_val <- cor(theo_quantiles, sample_quantiles)^2
  
  # B. Calculate Sample Absolute Skewness (3rd standardized moment)
  m3 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^3)
  s3 <- sd(sample_means)^3
  skew_val <- abs(m3 / s3)
  
  # C. Calculate Sample Absolute Excess Kurtosis (4th standardized moment - 3)
  m4 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^4)
  s4 <- sd(sample_means)^4
  kurt_val <- abs((m4 / s4) - 3)
  
  # Append to results data frame
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    n = n,
    R2 = r2_val,
    Skewness = skew_val,
    Excess_Kurtosis = kurt_val
  ))
}

# ==============================================================================
# Generate Diagnostic Plots with 3xSE Threshold Overlays
# ==============================================================================

# Graph 1: Q-Q Plot R^2 vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.98)
p1 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = R2)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.98, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.98, label = "Threshold (0.98)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("1. Quantile Alignment (" * R^2 * " vs. Sample Size)")),
    subtitle = expression("Six-Sided Die Parent"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = expression("Q-Q Plot " * R^2)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.95, 1.001)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph 2: Absolute Skewness vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.075)
p2 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Skewness)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkorange", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.075, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.075, label = "Threshold (0.075)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "2. Asymmetry (|Skewness| vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Six-Sided Die Parent"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "|Skewness|"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.1)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph 3: Absolute Excess Kurtosis vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.15)
p3 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Excess_Kurtosis)) +
  geom_line(color = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "forestgreen", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.15, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.15, label = "Threshold (0.15)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "3. Tail Weight (|Excess Kurtosis| vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Six-Sided Die Parent"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "|Excess Kurtosis|"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.7)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display diagnostic plots
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(p3)
```

R\^2 passes at between n=2 and n=5, skew always passes, and excess kurtosis passes between n=5 and n=10. Excess kurtosis is the last test to pass, so I will examine the n values between 5 and 10 closer to determine the exact value of n.

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# Refinement Simulation: Six-Sided Die (Excess Kurtosis Crossover)
# ==============================================================================


# 1. Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6418)

# 2. Simulation parameters
B <- 10000                            # Number of Monte Carlo repetitions
n_values <- 5:10                      # Fine-grained sample sizes

# 3. Initialize storage
results <- data.frame()


# 4. Run Monte Carlo loop
for (n in n_values) {
  
  # Draw B sample means from rolling n fair six-sided dice
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE)))
  
  # Save raw sample means to sim_data so n = 8 can be plotted in Chunk 3
  sim_data[[as.character(n)]] <- sample_means
  
  # Calculate Sample Absolute Excess Kurtosis (4th standardized moment - 3)
  m4 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^4)
  s4 <- sd(sample_means)^4
  kurt_val <- abs((m4 / s4) - 3)
  
  # Append to results data frame
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    n = n,
    Excess_Kurtosis = kurt_val
  ))
}

# ==============================================================================
# Generate Excess Kurtosis Plot with 0.15 Threshold Overlay
# ==============================================================================

p_kurtosis_zoom <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Excess_Kurtosis)) +
  geom_line(color = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "forestgreen", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.15, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.15, label = "Threshold (0.15)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "3. Tail Weight (|Excess Kurtosis| vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Six-Sided Die Parent"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "|Excess Kurtosis|"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display plot
print(p_kurtosis_zoom)
```

The lowest value of n that passes the kurtosis test is n=8.

```{r}
# Extract raw n = 2 sample means from sim_data list
df_n2 <- data.frame(sample_means = sim_data[["8"]])

# Graph v1: Histogram + Density (Multimodality Check)
v1 <- ggplot(df_n2, aes(x = sample_means)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
    binwidth = 1/8,
    center = 3.5,
    fill = "steelblue", 
    color = "white", 
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_density(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("Visual Check for Unimodality")),
    subtitle = expression("Sample Means at n = 8"),
    x = "Sample Mean",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph v2: Normal Q-Q Plot for n = 8
v2 <- ggplot(df_n2, aes(sample = sample_means)) +
  stat_qq(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("Normal Q-Q Plot")),
    subtitle = expression("Sample Means at n = 8"),
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display visual validation plots
print(v1)
print(v2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Conclusion

As expected, the n value for normality was quite low. This distribution highlights an interesting characteristic of discrete values when compared to continuous values. Because the individual results can only be integers from one two six, the means of the values can only ever be multiples of $\frac{1}{n}$, which leads to a visible staircasing effect on the Q-Q plot. However, the means still exhibit behavior indicative of a normal distribution.

$$\boxed{n=\text{8}}$$
